comment_content:
The course content is a well-structured survey of essential mathematical tools for business and social sciences. It is highly practical and application-oriented.
Part 1: Finance & Algebra (Ch. 3 & 4): The course starts with the mathematics of finance (simple/compound interest, annuities, amortization), which is immediately relevant for any business student. This is followed by an extensive unit on matrices and systems of linear equations. This section is fundamental for understanding data organization, solving multi-variable problems, and is a building block for more advanced topics like operations research.
Part 2: Differential Calculus (Ch. 10, 11, 12): This is the core of the course. It covers limits, the derivative, and all its applications. Key topics include various rules of differentiation (product, quotient, chain), implicit differentiation, and concepts like elasticity of demand. The most valuable part is applying derivatives to curve sketching and optimization (finding max profit, min cost), which are crucial for economic modeling and decision-making.
Part 3: Integral Calculus (Ch. 13 & 14): The course concludes with integration, covering antiderivatives, the fundamental theorem of calculus, and techniques like substitution. The applications to area between curves and analyzing probability density functions provide a strong foundation for economic analysis and statistics.
Overall: The content is demanding but incredibly useful. It doesn't delve into the deep theoretical proofs of higher-level calculus but focuses intensely on how to use these tools, which is exactly what a business student needs.

comment_content:
3 parts:
Basic Financial Mathematics (very easy)
Linear Algebra
Calculus
For the midterm:
It covers Financial Mathematics and Linear Algebra. Calculators are allowed. The midterm is not very difficult—if you study the lecturer’s handwritten notes thoroughly, you should easily secure at least 80% (at least based on this year’s paper).
The sample paper has a similar difficulty level to the actual midterm. Some questions follow exactly the same format as those in the sample paper or the examples shown in lectures, with only the numbers changed. So make sure you understand and remember the steps for every type of question.
For those who have never studied linear algebra before: don’t worry, it’s perfectly manageable. It’s just basic mathematics that requires a bit more time to get used to. Personally, I didn’t take M1/M2 in HKDSE and only got Level 4 in Maths, yet I found the midterm very easy.
For the final:
Calculus only. No calculator is allowed, but you may bring one double-sided A4 cheat sheet.
This is where things get really challenging. Calculus is taught starting around Week 7, leaving only about 5-6 weeks to prepare for a final exam that is worth 65% of the total grade. Unlike the earlier topics, calculus involves a lot of symbolic manipulation—lots of variables, exponents, subscripts, integrals, derivatives, and complicated equations—rather than straightforward numerical calculations. Many new concepts are introduced, and they can be quite difficult for beginners to grasp.
This year, the final paper was WAY MORE HARDER than the sample paper, so don’t be misled into thinking that memorising the solutions from the sample will be enough. It absolutely won’t.
The exam was genuinely tough—you’ll see what I mean when you look at the grade statistics below. To do well, you need to practise more difficult exercises from the textbook. The TA exercises, lecture examples, and sample paper are far too easy to prepare you adequately. Make sure you’re thoroughly prepared!

Wow, they actually did it, they have somehow managed to put every calculus thing in M2 in a 3-month course. Is it fun? I'll let you decide.
There are mainly 2 big topics: Preface, and Actual Calculus.
The first topic is Preface, which has a huge range of tiny stuff in it. From intervals, to composite functions, to some trigonometry stuff, and finally limits, stuff you have to understand before moving onto the actual "good" stuff. It can be overwhelming for some, but you really need to fully understand them (except trigo) before moving on, and there are couple ways to help with that, which I would talking more in the Workload section. Almost forgot, Squeeze Theorem and Intermediate Value Theorem, REMEMEBER THESE NAMES.
Here comes the big daddy: Actual Calculus. This course mostly discuss about Differentiation, from first principle, to all the rules, to implict differentiation, and finally related rates and optimization. It's honestly kinda fun to work around the problem, but unless you're a psychopath like me, you might not like it as much.
One more topic: Integration. There's honestly not a lot to talk about, only two main things to worry about: U-Substitution and fundemental theorem of calculus, and that's about it.
Overall, I do think as a 3-month course, it's a bit too much for most to handle, but if you are a psychopath who is curious about everything, I think you can have a fun time in this course. Personal view on content, B sounds pretty good.

This course (or 1013) is mandatory for all science students for good reason, as introductory calculus is important for many fields in STEM. The content in this course is pretty much identical to that of IB Math AASL. If you have no calculus background, be prepared to grind out practice problems for a good grade.
Even for people with a strong background in calculus, the final exam can be quite challenging, so make sure to attempt at least a few before going into the exam.
Some tips for doing well: 
- Having a strong precalculus (algebraic manipulations, trigonometry, etc.) foundation is important, so if you aren't confident, spend some time practicing the fundamentals before starting the course
- Getting a conceptual understanding of key calculus concepts is crucial for doing well. As such, I recommend watching the following playlist by 3b1b: https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLZHQObOWTQDMsr9K-rj53DwVRMYO3t5Yr
- Do as many past papers as you can, including the past papers for MATH1013. This is because the content covered in 1013 is practically identical to that in 1012, and there is a wider selection of 1013 papers to attempt.
Pre-midterm content:
- Elementary functions, intervals, continuity, limits, basic derivatives
Post-midterm content:
- Implicit differentiation, derivatives of inverse functions (trigonometric, logarithmic, etc.), related rates, optimization, mean value theorem, curve sketching, L'Hopital's rule, antiderivatives, definite integrals, FTC, integration by substitution

comment_grading:
Weighting:
10% WebWork
35% Midterm (1 hr 30 mins)
55% Final (3 hrs)
Both exams had around 30% MCQ and 70% LQ. Make sure to double check your answers, especially for MCQs, as a single error could drop you down a subgrade. The time given is plenty for both exams.
In my opinion, the midterm was far easier than the final. 
Absolute grading (though I heard the boundaries were relaxed a bit, possibly due to unexpectedly low exam scores):
A+/A/A- > 85% > B+/B/B- > 70% > C+/C/C- > 50% > D > 40% > F
Approximately 5% per sub grade, so 95% is required for A+, which is not easy.
Midterm: Mean: 57.79/102 SD: 22.84/102
Final: statistics not released
As you can see, the average grade is ~C, with around 40% of people getting a D. However, B range is easily attainable with enough practice (A+ is challenging due to the little margin of error).
comment_workload:
In terms of homework, there are a total of 8 WebWork assignments with around 20 questions each. Overall, the assignments took me around 1 to 2 hours each. You get unlimited attempts, so make sure to get 100% on all assignments to do well in the course.
In terms of revision, you will need to do past papers in order to do well. If you do not have a strong mathematics foundation, you'll need to try extra hard to get a good grade.
If you just want to pass, the workload is not bad at all.

The content itself is not too difficult, as it covers functions, derivatives and integration, focusing on mostly the theory behind how these work. However, as this is supposed to be a Maths Course for students who have no intention to take Maths, it feels quite boring, as the maths learned is useless. 
For example, the topic of Riemann Sum's are taught after Integration, even though its mostly a less efficient method to do the same thing and won't be needed for anyone who has a calculator. 
In other words, the content feels like it was designed for those who enjoy the problem-solving and theory of mathematics, rather than its application, yet anyone who is a Maths Major would be exempt from taking this course anyways.

comment_grading:
The grading is quite harsh and penalises small mistakes, making it a bit more difficult to get an A range grade. It is absolute grading, with each grade being around 15% intervals, e.g A range = 85%+, B range = 70-85% etc. 
The overall syllabus is weighted: 
Midterm: 35% 
Finals: 55%
Webwork: 10% 
There is an MCQ part in the Midterm and Finals, where each MCQ is weighted 5% and 3% respectively (the test is out of 100 for both). This makes it quite susceptible to careless mistakes or errors and can be quite unforgiving, on top of the fixed grading system. For our Midterm, the mean was under 60% which seems better than previous years at least.
comment_workload:

Here are some tips for reviewing:
To review Phyllis's notes, it's recommended to start by reviewing the concepts and theorems. If you find anything difficult to understand, you can refer to 水山哥's notes, which provide a more fundamental explanation.
